paragraphs: Drawing samples from a probability distribution with many dimensions is an important computational task. Langevin Monte Carlo approaches it through a stochastic dynamical process. This paper introduces a higher-order numerical method for that process, aiming to improve sampling accuracy while keeping each iteration relatively inexpensive.

The algorithm uses a stochastic Runge–Kutta method with strong order 1.5 for overdamped Langevin dynamics. It requires two gradient evaluations per iteration, compared with three in the earlier Runge–Kutta approach discussed in the abstract, and avoids computing Hessians. The contribution therefore combines a higher-order approximation with a reduction in the work required for each step.

Under specified log-smoothness conditions, the authors establish finite-time error bounds in Wasserstein-2 distance. They obtain a uniform-in-time rate of O(d^(3/2) h^(3/2)), where d is dimension and h is step size, in a setting that need not be log-concave. This matches the cited earlier rate while extending beyond its log-concavity condition. Numerical experiments also support the method’s effectiveness.
icml-2026-accelerating-langevin-monte-ca.tldr: A Hessian-free Langevin sampler uses two gradient evaluations per step and establishes higher-order convergence under conditions that allow non-log-concave distributions.

paragraphs: Systems made of multiple language-model agents can spend many tokens exchanging messages that do little to improve the final answer. AgentTailor addresses this by asking whether a communication connection contributes useful meaning to the decision. Its focus is the value of what agents exchange, beyond the arrangement of connections between them.

The framework uses an edge judgment mechanism to evaluate the semantic contribution of communication links. It also introduces an Edge Prediction Network that estimates the usefulness of these links through virtual execution without calling the language models. This provides a way to assess communication choices without paying for a full language-model interaction each time.

Across six datasets covering different fields, AgentTailor reports the best average accuracy, 91.36%, while reducing total token use by 21.2%–61.6%. These results support the practical value of measuring message contribution when optimizing agent communication. The approach ties communication cost to decision quality, making the usefulness of an exchange an explicit part of the system’s design.
icml-2026-agenttailor-a-semantic-aware-l.tldr: AgentTailor estimates which agent communications help the final decision, reducing token use while reporting the best average accuracy across six datasets.

paragraphs: A single noisy electron-microscopy projection does not uniquely determine a crystal’s atomic structure: different lattices can produce similar image contrast. AutoMat approaches reconstruction as a search over hypotheses that must undergo physical verification. Its controller connects image interpretation to the production of crystal structures suitable for simulation and downstream property calculations.

The system combines pattern-adaptive denoising, symmetry-constrained atomic reconstruction, and relaxation and validation using machine-learning interatomic potentials. Physics-guided template retrieval serves as an auxiliary branch whose use depends on the current state. When verification fails, the controller can roll back and retry, allowing physical feedback to influence the reconstruction process during inference.

The authors introduce STEM2Mat-Bench, containing more than 450 annotated samples, and assess lattice deviation, formation-energy error, and structure-matching accuracy. They report better performance than existing models, specialized tools, and closed-source multimodal models. The findings support a workflow in which reconstruction and physical checking work together to address ambiguity in microscopy, rather than treating the initial image interpretation as a finished structure.
icml-2026-automat-physics-guided-agentic.tldr: AutoMat searches and physically verifies crystal reconstructions from noisy microscopy images, retrying failed hypotheses to produce simulation-ready structures.

paragraphs: Code-generating language models usually append tokens to a prefix that remains fixed. This makes it difficult to revise an earlier choice while continuing to write the program. Stream of Revision changes the generation process so that producing new code and editing previous code can be interleaved within the model’s own decoding.

The method introduces action tokens that let the model backtrack and modify its history. The abstract describes these operations as occurring within a single forward pass, internalizing a revision loop that other approaches delegate to later agents or external tools. The model can therefore use its own semantic reasoning to respond to problems as code generation proceeds.

Experiments on secure code generation report a significant reduction in vulnerabilities with minimal inference overhead. This supports the idea that allowing revisions during decoding can make the model’s existing capabilities more useful for security. The stated result is improved vulnerability reduction in the evaluated setting; the method’s central contribution is making correction an explicit operation within code generation.
icml-2026-autoregressive-yet-revisable-i.tldr: Stream of Revision lets a code model edit its own earlier output during decoding, reducing vulnerabilities with minimal reported inference overhead.

paragraphs: Dense language models increase computational cost as they grow because every parameter participates in processing every token. This paper explores increasing capacity through mixtures of complete processing streams across the language-model pipeline. The aim is to extend mixture-style scaling beyond its usual concentration in feed-forward modules.

The authors establish an equivalence between mixture-of-experts layers and dynamic convolutions with variable kernels. Each expert corresponds to a 1×1 convolutional kernel, while routing combines kernels according to the input. cMoLLM builds on this formulation to route across end-to-end streams through fully differentiable dynamic convolution, providing a common mechanism for learning how streams contribute.

In GPT-2-style models trained on FineWeb, cMoLLM improves language-modeling perplexity and performance on GLUE and SQuAD under matched compute. The authors also report better stream utilization, more stable optimization, and favorable scaling relative to ParaScale- and AltUp-style baselines. These findings support the proposed routing formulation in the tested model setting and connect its quality gains to more effective use of parallel streams.
icml-2026-cmollm-at-scale-horizontal-sca.tldr: cMoLLM uses dynamic convolution to route across complete language-model streams, improving quality and stream utilization under matched compute in GPT-2-style experiments.

paragraphs: Designing D-peptides that bind L-proteins requires a model to handle interactions between molecules with different handedness. The paper studies whether training on L-peptide–L-protein interactions can support this different design task. This matters because D-peptide binders have therapeutic potential, while their generation has received relatively little attention in machine-learning peptide design.

The proposed method adds axial features to the polar vector features of an E(3)-equivariant model. The authors show that this representation change makes generalization from same-handed training interactions to differently handed design interactions feasible. They implement the approach within a latent diffusion model to generate new D-peptide binders conditioned on protein targets.

The resulting designs outperform existing tools in computational benchmarks and demonstrate efficacy in laboratory validation. The authors describe the model, to their knowledge, as the first experimentally validated AI generative approach for designing D-peptide binders from scratch. The findings support the value of explicitly representing chirality when transferring learned interaction patterns across molecular handedness.
icml-2026-cross-chirality-generalization.tldr: Adding axial features enables a peptide diffusion model trained on L-L interactions to design D-peptide binders with computational and laboratory validation.

paragraphs: A training example’s usefulness can change as a model learns. Data Agent treats the choice of training samples as a sequence of decisions that should adapt alongside model optimization. This addresses the weakness of selection rules based on fixed importance scores, occasional snapshots, or metrics handcrafted for a particular task.

The agent learns a policy for selecting individual samples using a reward that combines two signals: difficulty measured through loss and uncertainty measured through confidence. These signals represent complementary goals of influencing optimization and gaining information. An adaptive weighting mechanism balances them over training without requiring tuning of that balance.

Experiments across datasets and architectures report faster training while maintaining or improving performance. On ImageNet-1k and MMLU, the authors report cost reductions exceeding 50% without performance loss. The framework also addresses scenarios involving noisy datasets. Its dataset-independent formulation and modular reward make the selection strategy adaptable across tasks, while the results show that tracking changing sample utility can reduce training effort substantially.
icml-2026-data-agent-learning-to-select-.tldr: Data Agent learns an evolving sample-selection policy that accelerates training, with reported cost reductions above 50% without performance loss on ImageNet-1k and MMLU.

paragraphs: Decentralized federated learning lets connected clients train collaboratively without a central server. Simply averaging their model parameters can compromise update directions and limit exploration of possible solutions. Exchanging whole layers offers more exploration, but the resulting diversity in update directions can also make training unstable.

DecFus combines layer exchange and averaging within one framework. It uses pairwise cosine similarity to divide layers into an exchange group for exploration and an averaging group for exploitation. Loss variance among neighboring clients guides a transition from exploration-dominated training toward greater exploitation, adjusting the balance as learning progresses.

The authors establish convergence without requiring the aggregation matrix to be doubly stochastic, a common assumption in existing analyses. Experiments report superior performance against centralized and decentralized federated methods when client data are both identically and non-identically distributed. The contribution connects a practical strategy for managing diverse updates with a convergence analysis that removes this particular aggregation requirement, supporting more flexible decentralized training.
icml-2026-decfus-decentralized-layer-wis.tldr: DecFus dynamically combines layer exchange and averaging to improve decentralized training and proves convergence without a doubly stochastic aggregation requirement.

paragraphs: Applying an artistic style to a 3D scene requires the appearance to remain coherent across viewpoints. DiffStyle3D targets this problem for scenes represented by 3D Gaussian splatting. It uses diffusion-model representations while directly optimizing in latent space, addressing the training instability associated with approaches that rely on denoising directions.

Its Attention-Aware Loss aligns style information in self-attention features and separately aligns content features to preserve the scene’s original content. Geometry is also incorporated into self-attention so that the model can connect corresponding regions across views. This makes the scene’s spatial structure part of the mechanism used to coordinate stylization.

A geometry-aware mask further prevents redundant optimization where views overlap. Together, these components link appearance changes across viewpoints while avoiding repeated treatment of the same regions. Experiments report better stylization quality and visual realism than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support using attention features and explicit geometric correspondence as complementary tools for producing consistent stylized 3D content.
icml-2026-diffstyle3d-consistent-3d-gaus.tldr: DiffStyle3D combines attention-based style alignment with geometric correspondence to improve the quality and cross-view consistency of stylized 3D Gaussian scenes.

paragraphs: A language model attempting a formal proof needs useful feedback when verification fails. ExVerus focuses on giving it concrete examples of program behavior that explain the failure. This addresses a weakness of approaches that predict proofs directly from source code and receive only limited feedback from the verifier.

When a proof fails, ExVerus automatically generates counterexamples and validates them. It then guides the language model to generalize those examples into inductive invariants: conditions intended to remain true as execution proceeds. The counterexamples ground this repair process in specific failures, while the invariants aim to rule out the broader patterns those failures reveal.

The evaluation reports significant improvements in proof accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency compared with a state-of-the-art prompting-based Verus proof generator. These results support using behavioral feedback to guide proof repair. The distinctive step is moving from a concrete failing case to a general condition that can help the verifier establish correctness, giving the model a more informative basis for its next proof attempt.
icml-2026-exverus-verus-proof-repair-via.tldr: ExVerus turns validated counterexamples into guidance for repairing Verus proofs, improving reported accuracy, robustness, and token efficiency.

paragraphs: A changing graph can contain hierarchical, grid-like, and cyclic neighborhoods at the same time. Their shapes can also change as nodes and connections appear or disappear. DyGMoCE addresses the mismatch that arises when all these structures must be represented in a space with one fixed curvature.

The model adds curvature-aware experts to both the attention and feed-forward parts of a dynamic graph Transformer. Each expert operates on a Riemannian manifold with a different curvature, allowing each node’s representation space to adapt at each timestamp. A routing mechanism with a ranking constraint uses the geometric continuity between experts to guide their selection.

The paper also introduces fast Riemannian attention, reporting an average speedup of 27.5% and memory reduction of 52.6%. This attention module is described as applicable more broadly to Transformers processing sequences. Experiments show significant improvements over other state-of-the-art graph methods. The work therefore combines more adaptable representation geometry with an efficiency improvement for the attention computation supporting it.
icml-2026-fast-mixture-of-curvature-awar.tldr: DyGMoCE adapts representation curvature to changing graph neighborhoods and introduces faster, more memory-efficient Riemannian attention.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models can choose the order in which they fill missing positions. Existing samplers often favor tokens that already appear most certain. The paper shows that this local strategy can leave greater uncertainty across the remaining generation, because an easy immediate choice may do little to clarify what comes next.

The Info-Gain Sampler balances uncertainty at the position being filled with the information that choice provides about positions still masked. It uses the model’s bidirectional structure to account for these downstream effects. Because the method is training-free, its contribution lies in changing the decoding procedure rather than learning a new model.

Across reasoning, coding, creative writing, and image generation, the authors report consistent improvements over existing masked-diffusion samplers. Average reasoning accuracy increases by 2.9–11.6 percentage points, and creative-writing comparisons yield a 62.8% average win rate. These findings support treating decoding order as an information-management decision: useful choices can help organize the unresolved parts of an output as well as resolve the current position.
icml-2026-improving-sampling-for-masked-.tldr: The training-free Info-Gain Sampler improves masked-diffusion generation by considering how each decoding choice reduces uncertainty in remaining positions.

paragraphs: Increasing a language model’s capacity usually brings additional computation, while mixture-of-experts designs introduce memory and hardware-efficiency challenges. This paper investigates token-indexed parameters as another way to scale capacity. The idea is to add parameters whose use requires very little arithmetic, creating a scaling direction complementary to existing architectures.

ReToken and MoRT retrieve modulation vectors from auxiliary embedding tables and apply them within Transformer layers. Lightweight element-wise operations use these vectors to modulate the backbone, adding negligible floating-point computation. The approach is evaluated on both dense and mixture-of-experts models spanning 190 million to 9.8 billion parameters.

Experiments report consistent validation-loss reductions and improved downstream results, including gains of 7.3 on ARC-C and 6.3 on GSM8K. Compute-controlled analysis finds that MoRT achieves comparable quality with 35% less compute than vanilla mixture-of-experts architectures. The authors also observe predictable power-law scaling for token-indexed parameters and marginal implementation overhead. Together, these results support modulation tables as an additional practical way to improve quality per unit of compute.
icml-2026-inner-layer-token-self-modulat.tldr: ReToken and MoRT add token-indexed modulation parameters with little computation, with MoRT matching vanilla MoE quality using 35% less compute in the reported analysis.

paragraphs: Understanding a cell’s future fate requires separating differentiation signals from other biological activity, such as the cell cycle. Lineage-aware Contrastive Learning uses inheritable lineage barcodes to help make that separation. These barcodes provide naturally occurring relationships that can guide learning toward subtle signals associated with cellular ancestry and fate.

The framework treats lineage information as a natural form of data augmentation for contrastive learning. Its semi-supervised architecture also aligns cells without lineage labels, allowing learned lineage structure to transfer to clinical datasets that lack explicit barcoding. This connects the richer supervision available in lineage-tracing data with settings where that information cannot be directly observed.

The authors demonstrate prediction of future cell-type compositions from early observations, using cross-sectional data to model fate commitment over time. On hematopoietic and fibroblast systems, LCL significantly outperforms standard models including scVI. These findings support lineage-informed representations for studying differentiation, while the potential to manipulate cell fate remains a prospective application of improved understanding.
icml-2026-leveraging-lineage-barcodes-as.tldr: LCL uses inherited lineage barcodes to learn fate-related cell representations and improve predictions of future cell-type composition.

paragraphs: Online optimization in a changing environment needs a performance measure that allows the best decision to change over time. Switching regret sums the static regret within segments of the time horizon, for an arbitrary partition into segments. This paper asks whether stronger convexity properties permit logarithmic switching-regret bounds.

The authors introduce IRESET, a meta-algorithm that combines decisions from multiple experts operating over different intervals. Its aggregation procedure uses second-order bounds to combine those decisions sequentially. A segment-tree structure organizes the analysis across the full horizon, with recursive equations helping relate performance on individual intervals to the overall switching regret.

With appropriate expert algorithms, IRESET achieves logarithmic switching-regret bounds for exponentially concave and strongly convex functions. This resolves the stated open question for those function classes, extending the available theory beyond the general-convex setting discussed in the abstract. The significance is conditional on the objective’s structure: the framework shows how suitable experts and interval aggregation can exploit these stronger properties in non-stationary online optimization.
icml-2026-logarithmic-switching-regret-f.tldr: IRESET combines interval-based experts to obtain logarithmic switching-regret bounds for exponentially concave and strongly convex online objectives.

paragraphs: Interactive virtual worlds need objects with functional and physical properties, as well as convincing geometry. PhysForge addresses asset generation by making those properties part of the design process. The framework separates planning how an object should function from generating its geometry and motion parameters.

In the first stage, a vision-language model produces a hierarchical physical blueprint specifying material, functional, and kinematic constraints. In the second, a physics-grounded diffusion model turns that plan into detailed geometry together with kinematic parameters. A mechanism called KineVoxel Injection supports this joint generation, connecting the planned physical behavior to the resulting asset.

The framework is supported by PhysDB, a dataset of 150,000 assets with four tiers of physical annotations. Experiments show that PhysForge produces functionally plausible assets ready for simulation. These findings support organizing generation around functional logic and hierarchical physics. The resulting assets are intended to provide content for interactive environments and embodied agents, linking visual construction with the information needed for interaction.
icml-2026-physforge-generating-physics-g.tldr: PhysForge plans physical and functional constraints before generating 3D geometry and motion parameters, producing simulation-ready interactive assets.

paragraphs: Some neural-network optimizers depend on matrix operations such as square roots and orthogonalization. Computing these operations efficiently matters for overall training speed. PRISM accelerates iterative matrix-function algorithms that mainly use matrix multiplications, preserving an approach suited to modern GPUs without requiring explicit eigendecomposition.

At each iteration, PRISM adapts a polynomial approximation to the matrix’s current spectrum. It does this through a randomized sketch and a least-squares fitting problem, keeping the adaptation overhead small. The framework does not require explicit spectral bounds or singular-value estimates, so it can adjust to the instance as the spectrum evolves.

The authors apply PRISM to Newton–Schulz-like iterations for matrix square roots and orthogonalization. When incorporated into the Shampoo and Muon optimizers, it empirically accelerates neural-network training. The contribution therefore reaches beyond speeding up an isolated numerical operation: it demonstrates that adaptive approximation of the matrix functions used inside optimizers can translate into faster training in the evaluated integrations.
icml-2026-prism-distribution-free-adapti.tldr: PRISM adaptively fits polynomial matrix-function approximations using randomized sketches, accelerating training when integrated into Shampoo and Muon.

paragraphs: A language model’s bounded context limits how much reasoning it can actively hold at once. This paper proposes recursive models that can call themselves to solve subtasks in isolated contexts. The approach gives each subtask its own working context, making recursive decomposition a central part of the reasoning process.

The authors prove that every computable problem admits a recursive reasoning decomposition whose subtasks need exponentially smaller active context than standard autoregressive models. Within their analysis, this surpasses context management restricted to one sequence, including summarization. They also extend the framework to agentic systems with arbitrary context processing and control flow, proving that recursive models can attain optimal power within that broader class.

Experimentally, a trained three-billion-parameter recursive model significantly outperforms frontier language models on Boolean satisfiability, a task involving extended combinatorial search. The theoretical result concerns the existence and power of recursive decompositions; the experiment demonstrates a learned realization on a demanding search problem. Together, they make recursion a concrete direction for extending reasoning beyond a single bounded context.
icml-2026-recursive-models-for-long-hori.tldr: Recursive self-calls enable provable active-context savings, and a trained 3B recursive model outperforms frontier LLMs on Boolean satisfiability.

paragraphs: A language model’s key–value cache helps reuse prior computation, but its memory cost becomes a bottleneck for long contexts. This paper frames eviction as a problem of preserving useful information within a smaller retained cache. It seeks a shared theoretical objective behind policies that are often designed as empirical heuristics.

Under a linear–Gaussian surrogate for attention, the authors derive a closed-form mutual-information objective describing a retained subset’s effective information capacity. The formulation interprets several existing eviction strategies as approximations to capacity maximization. This theoretical connection depends on the surrogate model used in the derivation.

The proposed CapKV method targets information preservation through a log-determinant approximation using statistical leverage scores. These tools translate the capacity objective into a practical selection mechanism. Across multiple models and long-context benchmarks, CapKV consistently outperforms prior approaches in the reported experiments, offering a better balance between memory use and generation fidelity. The findings support using an explicit information objective to guide which cached content remains available.
icml-2026-rethinking-kv-cache-eviction-v.tldr: CapKV uses an information-capacity objective derived under a linear–Gaussian attention surrogate to improve the memory–quality trade-off in cache eviction.

paragraphs: Safety alignment can become fragile when deployment conditions change or preference labels are noisy. This paper argues that uncertainty in the training data is only part of the problem: the geometry of preference optimization can itself introduce fragility. ShaPO targets this optimization behavior within the parameters most important for alignment.

The framework applies selective geometry control to an alignment-critical parameter subspace while enforcing worst-case alignment objectives. Avoiding uniform constraints helps reduce over-regularization that can harm robustness under distribution shift. A token-level version stabilizes likelihood-based surrogate optimization, while a reward-level version aims to maintain reward-consistent optimization with noisy supervision.

Across safety benchmarks and noisy-preference settings, ShaPO consistently improves robustness compared with popular preference-optimization methods. Combining it with objectives designed for data robustness produces additional gains. These results empirically support treating optimization geometry as a complementary source of robustness improvements: changes to how the objective is optimized can add value alongside methods that address uncertainty in the preference data.
icml-2026-revisiting-robustness-for-llm-.tldr: ShaPO selectively controls optimization geometry in alignment-critical parameters, improving empirical safety robustness under distribution shift and noisy preferences.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval models can struggle with noisy queries. Updating them at test time using only confident predictions risks reinforcing existing mistakes and discarding useful evidence from ambiguous queries. ReEx extends adaptation across the query stream by combining repairs to textual input with learning signals that remain usable when the correct match is uncertain.

Its Generative Semantic Refinement module uses language-model repairs to address structural noise in text. Confidence-guided dynamic fusion anchors those repairs to prevent changes in meaning. A second component learns through exclusion sets of unlikely candidates, imposing negative constraints instead of requiring an ambiguous query to supply a confident positive match.

Experiments on COCO-C and Flickr-C show consistent improvements over existing test-time adaptation methods, with significant robustness gains and a computational trade-off described by the authors as justified. The approach makes low-confidence queries useful through evidence about what they are unlikely to match. Combining that exclusion signal with controlled text repair provides two complementary ways to address noisy retrieval.
icml-2026-robust-cross-modal-retrieval-v.tldr: ReEx improves noisy cross-modal retrieval by controlling language-model query repairs and learning from unlikely matches even when queries are ambiguous.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning often depends on relationships between objects, yet multimodal models can focus on objects in isolation. Scene Graph Thinking, or SaGe, gives models an explicit structure for reasoning about entities and their relationships. The goal is to improve fine-grained perception and make navigation toward relevant visual targets more efficient.

An automated data engine converts image–text examples into scene graphs, with hierarchical entities as nodes and visual relations as edges. The authors sample reasoning traces from these graphs to construct 120,000 training examples. This turns existing flat image–text material into supervision that exposes how visual entities connect.

Training proceeds in two stages: supervised fine-tuning teaches structured reasoning, and reinforcement fine-tuning uses node-as-proxy graph rewards to strengthen efficient graph exploration. The approach produces significant improvements across eight multimodal benchmarks. These findings support coordinating the structure of training data with the reward used for reasoning, so that both stages encourage the model to use relationships when interpreting visually demanding inputs.
icml-2026-scene-graph-thinking-reinforci.tldr: SaGe trains multimodal models with scene-graph reasoning traces and graph-based rewards, improving fine-grained visual reasoning across eight benchmarks.

paragraphs: Neural operators approximate solutions to partial differential equations and must capture interactions between distant spatial points. In many PDE regimes, these global interactions are empirically compressible: their spectra decay quickly enough to support low-rank approximations. This paper uses that observation to organize several global-mixing approaches under a common computational template.

The template compresses spatial features into a compact latent space, processes global interactions there, and reconstructs contextual information at the original points. Low-Rank Spatial Attention directly implements this pattern using standard attention, normalization, and feed-forward networks. Its construction makes it straightforward to implement and compatible with hardware-optimized Transformer kernels.

Experiments show that this relatively simple design achieves high accuracy, with average error more than 17% below the second-best methods, while remaining stable and efficient during mixed-precision training. The findings support compact latent interaction as an effective design principle in the tested settings. The motivating compressibility observation applies to many PDE regimes, providing a stated basis for the low-rank approach.
icml-2026-simple-yet-effective-low-rank-.tldr: LRSA uses standard Transformer components for low-rank spatial interaction, reporting over 17% lower average error than second-best methods in its experiments.

paragraphs: Natural image corruptions can undermine a vision model’s reliability. This paper examines robustness through the internal computational pathways that carry features across network layers. The authors identify a progressive decline in robust features through those layers and establish a functional relationship between their prevalence and model performance.

Suppress and Diversify uses these observations to refine the model’s pathways explicitly. It dynamically selects robust pathways and diversifies them with symmetry-preserving transformations. The approach is described as non-intrusive, architecture-agnostic, and parameter-free, with no additional computation at test time. This makes the pathway-level intervention relevant to robustness without adding an inference-time processing burden.

Evaluations across eight benchmarks report consistent performance improvements spanning multiple vision tasks, different backbone architectures, and complex real-world scenarios. The findings support the idea that robustness depends partly on how robust features survive and propagate inside a network. They also show that explicitly refining those routes can improve evaluated performance across varied settings, rather than relying only on implicit representation learning.
icml-2026-suppress-and-diversify-refinin.tldr: Suppress and Diversify improves corruption robustness by selecting and diversifying robust computational pathways without extra parameters or test-time overhead.

paragraphs: Image-watermark evaluation needs to assess both quality and security, while accounting for different watermark types. WMVLM provides a unified framework based on vision-language models that also generates interpretable explanations. It addresses evaluation practices that use unsuitable measures for semantic watermarks or return scores without explaining their meaning.

The framework assigns different criteria to the two watermark categories. Residual watermarks are assessed through artifact strength and resistance to erasure, while semantic watermarks are assessed through shifts in latent distributions. This distinction lets the evaluation reflect how each type is represented instead of forcing both into the same measurement scheme.

A three-stage training strategy progressively develops classification, scoring, and explanatory text generation. Experiments show that WMVLM outperforms state-of-the-art vision-language models and generalizes strongly across datasets, diffusion models, and watermarking methods. The reported contribution is an evaluator that combines type-appropriate assessment with readable explanations, making its judgments more informative for watermark development while incorporating security alongside image quality.
icml-2026-wmvlm-evaluating-diffusion-mod.tldr: WMVLM evaluates residual and semantic image watermarks with type-specific quality and security measures while generating interpretable explanations.
